summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Constitution permits a Rhode Island DCYF caseworker to take temporary custody of a child without a hearing when the caseworker has a reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or is imminent, and the DCYF worker here met that standard, so qualified immunity barred the claim.
key_cases.relevance: Hatch is the case a Rhode Island lawyer must satisfy or defeat on any emergency-removal question in federal court.
key_cases.quote: It follows, therefore, that a parent's right to the care, custody, and control of a minor child is inviolate unless a case worker has such a suspicion.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: A parent's familial-integrity right includes the right to prompt post-deprivation process after an emergency separation; the state actor who prolonged the separation without any hearing was not entitled to qualified immunity at summary judgment, while the prosecutor was.
key_cases.relevance: Suboh supplies the procedural half of the removal analysis that Hatch leaves open: exigency justifies the taking, but not the keeping.
key_cases.quote: Even when there are such exigent circumstances, there must be an adequate post-deprivation hearing within a reasonable time.

key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the Court set out the ex parte petition, preliminary hearing and probable-cause hearing sequence under § 40-11-7.1 and held that the twelve-month period for termination may run from the child's placement in DCYF care rather than from a formal finding of abuse or neglect.
key_cases.relevance: The seven-day preliminary hearing is the state-law deadline that follows any ex parte removal order.
key_cases.quote: Next, a hearing on the petition must be held within seven days.

key_cases.holding: Abuse and neglect findings were affirmed on medical evidence of fourteen non-accidental fractures, and the mother's Fourteenth Amendment challenge to DCYF's seventy-two-hour hold was not preserved because the parents waived the Rule 15(c)(5) probable-cause hearing.
key_cases.relevance: A constitutional challenge to an emergency hold must be raised at the probable-cause hearing or it is waived.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, we conclude that Kimberly's challenge to the temporary hold on the children was not preserved for appeal.

key_cases.case_name: Carter ex rel. Caleb O. v. Lindgren
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for Rhode Island DCYF officers was affirmed because, applying Hatch, the officers had an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse when they took the children into temporary custody, so no constitutional violation occurred.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading First Circuit application of Hatch to an actual DCYF emergency removal decision.
key_cases.quote: We need not address the latter two aspects of the Hatch test because we conclude that plaintiffs have not established a constitutional violation.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A State may not take children from a parent on a presumption of unfitness; every parent, including an unwed father, is entitled to a hearing on fitness before the children are removed, and denying that hearing violates due process and equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency removal by DCYF is an exception to, not a substitute for, the hearing on fitness this case guarantees, so the exigency justification must be made on the record promptly after the seizure.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.
